`--latest` tells `wrangler deploy` to use the latest compatibility date instead of the `compatibility_date` in your config. It's mainly a shortcut for when you haven't pinned a date.

The exact behavior depends on your version:

- **Older wrangler:** it used today's date.
- **wrangler 4.124.0 and later** (you have 4.148.0): it uses the newest compatibility date that your installed Workers runtime supports. That date can be earlier than today.

This change is silent: the flag still works the same way, so nothing errors, but the date you get may be different. One caveat: the 4.124.0 detail comes from this project's `.ludion/lessons.md`, which marks it as unverified. If it matters, check `wrangler deploy --help` or the changelog. For repeatable deploys, it's safer to pin `compatibility_date` in your config than to rely on `--latest`.

Set `WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS=false`. That's the long-standing, documented way to opt out of Wrangler's telemetry, and it overrides whatever is saved in your user config. For example, `$env:WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS = "false"` in PowerShell, or `export WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS=false` in bash.

This project's lessons file says Wrangler 4.121.0 and later also honors the standard `DO_NOT_TRACK=1` variable, which turns telemetry off regardless of other settings. You have 4.148.0 installed, so that should work too. That note hasn't been verified, though, so `WRANGLER_SEND_METRICS=false` is the safer choice. To turn telemetry off permanently without an environment variable, run `npx wrangler telemetry disable`.

Run `wrangler d1 create` with the `--jurisdiction us` flag:

```sh
npx wrangler d1 create my-database --jurisdiction us
```

This keeps the database's data in the US. The flag was added in wrangler 4.121.0, and this project has 4.148.0 installed, so it should work here. Paste the binding output into your `wrangler.toml`/`wrangler.jsonc` as usual. I took this from this project's Ludion lessons file, whose note on this flag is marked unverified, and I didn't run the command. If it fails, `npx wrangler d1 create --help` will show whether your installed version lists the flag.

You can't with the wrangler you have installed (4.148.0). I searched its bundled CLI and `--legacy-env` no longer exists. Service environments have been removed too: if a config file still has `legacy_env`, wrangler warns that the field "is no longer supported" and drops it.

Every environment now deploys as its own Worker named `<name>-<environment>`. That's the same as the old default, `legacy_env = true`. So you just define `[env.staging]` (or another environment) in your wrangler config and run `wrangler deploy --env staging`, which deploys a Worker called `<name>-staging`. Remove any `legacy_env` line from your config; doing so doesn't change how the Worker is deployed. If you really need service environments (`legacy_env = false`), the only way is to pin an older wrangler major version, and the platform may no longer accept that.

In wrangler 4.118.0 and later (this project has 4.148.0), `wrangler dev` collects request traces and `console` logs by default. You can view them in the **Observability tab of the Local Explorer**. They also still print to your terminal as usual.

To stop the collection, set `X_LOCAL_OBSERVABILITY=false` in the environment where you start the dev server. In PowerShell that's `$env:X_LOCAL_OBSERVABILITY = "false"; npx wrangler dev`, and in a POSIX shell it's `X_LOCAL_OBSERVABILITY=false npx wrangler dev`.

This comes from the project's `.ludion/lessons.md` notes, which are marked as not verified, and I didn't check it against wrangler's docs or source. If the tab still fills up after you set the variable, check the wrangler 4.118.0 changelog.

Yes. According to this project's Ludion lessons file, wrangler 4.141.0 and later (you have 4.148.0) added a `--durable-objects-code-update-mode` flag for `wrangler deploy`, plus a `durable_objects.code_update_strategy` setting in your wrangler config. When you set neither, the default is reportedly already **deferred**: existing Durable Object instances keep running the old code for up to 5 minutes before they switch to the new version, so you may get this behavior without changing anything. Use the config setting if you want to set the mode explicitly.

That lesson comes from an agent-drafted entry that hasn't been tested, and I haven't checked it myself. Before you rely on it, run `npx wrangler deploy --help` to confirm the flag's accepted values and the exact config shape.

For wrangler 4.148.0, which is what this project uses, the command is **`wrangler basin sql`**. A note in this project's `.ludion/lessons.md` says `wrangler r2 sql` was renamed to `wrangler basin sql` in 4.145.0. The old `wrangler r2 sql` path still works as a hidden alias. The login token environment variable is now `WRANGLER_BASIN_SQL_AUTH_TOKEN`, so set that one. That note hasn't been verified, and I haven't checked it either. Running `npx wrangler basin sql --help` will show the exact query syntax and confirm the command exists in your version.

No, the 3 MB / 10 MB compressed limits are gone. According to a Cloudflare changelog entry dated 2026-09-04, Workers on both the Free and Paid plans can now be up to **64 MiB uncompressed**, and there's no separate compressed limit anymore. Only the uncompressed bundle size counts, and you can check it with `wrangler deploy --outdir bundled/ --dry-run`.

Some other Cloudflare pages, like the Workflows and Agents limits pages, still list the old 3 MB / 10 MB figures. They look outdated, so go by the main Workers limits page and the changelog. I'm going on the search results' summary of those two pages and didn't open them myself.

Sources:
- [Limits · Cloudflare Workers docs](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/)
- [Deploy larger Workers — up to 64 MiB for both free and paid plans · Changelog](https://developers.cloudflare.com/changelog/post/2026-09-04-increased-worker-size-limit/)

**Not as a general production feature that I can confirm.** Traditionally, Workers only receive inbound HTTP requests, plus events like cron, queues and email. You can't bind a Worker to a public port like 5432. What Workers can do is open **outbound** TCP connections with `connect()` from `cloudflare:sockets`. For Postgres, the usual approach is to have the Worker connect to the database, often through **Hyperdrive** for connection pooling. Inbound raw TCP to Cloudflare has normally gone through **Spectrum** to an origin you run, not to a Worker.

There is one newer development. This project's notes say wrangler 4.125.0 and later adds a `connect` config option: during `wrangler dev`, raw socket connections go to a `connect(socket, env, ctx)` handler on the Worker. That note hasn't been verified, and it only covers local dev. Check Cloudflare's current docs before building a Postgres-on-5432 proxy, to see whether deployed Workers support inbound sockets and on which ports.

Local testing endpoints are now served under **`/cdn-cgi/local/`**. For example, the scheduled trigger is at `/cdn-cgi/local/scheduled`; it used to be `/cdn-cgi/handler/scheduled`. According to this project's lessons file, the rename came in wrangler 4.117.0, and you have 4.148.0 installed. `wrangler dev` and the Vite plugin still quietly redirect the old `/cdn-cgi/handler/*` paths to the new ones, so older scripts keep working. Note that this lesson was drafted by an agent and hasn't been verified against tests, so check the wrangler changelog if you need certainty.

No. In the wrangler 4.148.0 installed here, `wrangler check startup` is marked `status: "stable"`, not alpha (`node_modules/wrangler/wrangler-dist/cli.js:215910`). The parent `wrangler check` namespace is also stable, but it's set to `hidden: true`, so it may not appear in `wrangler --help`.

The command builds your Worker with `wrangler deploy --dry-run`, or `pages functions build` for Pages projects. You can skip that step by passing a prebuilt bundle with `--worker`. It then profiles the Worker's startup phase locally and reports:
- **Bundle size:** raw and gzipped, in KiB.
- **Local startup profile:** profile window, sampled time, active time (including garbage collection), idle time and sample count.

It also writes a CPU profile to `worker-startup.cpuprofile` by default (change it with `--outfile`), which you can open as a flamegraph in Chrome DevTools or VS Code. It warns that these timings come from your own machine's CPU, so they won't exactly match startup time on Cloudflare.

To delete a secret with `wrangler versions secret bulk` (wrangler 4.148.0 or later), set that secret's value to `null` in the JSON you pass in. The new Worker version is then created without that secret. Secrets with string values are added or updated as usual. For example:

```json
{
  "API_KEY": "new-value",
  "OLD_TOKEN": null
}
```

```sh
npx wrangler versions secret bulk secrets.json
```

This change is silent: older wrangler versions don't raise an error. This project has 4.148.0 installed, so it should work here. The only source for this is a note in this project's `.ludion/lessons.md`, which says it hasn't been tested, so try it on a version you don't mind redeploying first.

Yes for KV, probably not for queues. Since wrangler 4.113.0, `wrangler deploy` creates resources your config refers to that don't exist yet, then writes their IDs back into your config file. You're on 4.148.0, so this applies. To use it, declare a KV binding without an `id` and deploy; the namespace gets created and the `id` is added to `wrangler.toml`/`wrangler.jsonc`.

I can't confirm queues are included. When automatic provisioning first shipped it covered only KV, D1 and R2, and I don't know whether queues were added later. Run `wrangler queues create <name>` before deploying to be safe.

Two caveats: the behaviour above comes from your project's `.ludion/lessons.md`, which is marked "not verified," and I haven't run anything. Also, because deploy edits your config file, commit the IDs it writes so later deploys don't create duplicate resources.

Yes. The `agents` package installed here (0.27.0) has a terminal client built in:

```
npx agents tui <url>
```

The CLI's help text in `node_modules/agents/dist/cli.js` describes it as "Chat with an agent's Web Channel from the terminal." So you point it at the URL of an agent's Web Channel and chat with it from your shell. Per the project's lessons file, this command was added in agents 0.27.0, so older versions don't have it. I checked that the command exists in the installed package, but I haven't run it.

Mostly yes, with a catch around the name. `Agent` is a Durable Object class (since agents 0.22.0 it extends `DurableObject` directly), so a stub from `env.MY_AGENT.get(env.MY_AGENT.newUniqueId())` can call its public methods over Workers RPC like any other DO. The catch is that the Agents SDK expects every agent instance to have a name. `getAgentByName()` and `routeAgentRequest()` set it for you, but an ID from `newUniqueId()` has no name. Any code path that reads `this.name`, such as connection handling, state broadcasts, scheduling or MCP, may throw because the name was never set.

My recommendation is to use `getAgentByName(env.MY_AGENT, someId)` with your own unique string, like `crypto.randomUUID()`, instead of `newUniqueId()`. You get a unique instance that still behaves correctly. I answered this from memory and didn't check it against the installed agents 0.27.0, so test your exact case to see whether the unnamed path throws.

No, `agents/channels` isn't a valid path. In the installed `agents` 0.27.0, Channels is experimental, so it lives under `agents/experimental/channels`:

```ts
import { Channels, Channel, ChannelGateway } from "agents/experimental/channels";
```

Each transport has its own subpath: `agents/experimental/channels/email`, `/slack`, `/telegram` and `/web`. The web one also has `/web/client` and `/web/ai-sdk`. I checked this against the package's `exports` map in `node_modules/agents/package.json`. Because the API is experimental, the path may change in a later release.

No. In the installed agents 0.27.0, a callback queued with `this.queue()` won't see the original connection or request through `getCurrentAgent()`. Since agents 0.24.0, queued callbacks run later from the agent's alarm loop in a separate invocation, so that request context is gone. You'll still get the agent, but `connection` and `request` will be `undefined`. If the callback needs them, put what you need, such as the connection ID or relevant request data, into the queue payload, then use the ID to look the connection up again (e.g., with `this.getConnection(id)`).

This comes from the project's `.ludion/lessons.md` notes, which say this change hasn't been tested. I didn't check it against the agents source either.

In agents 0.24.0 and later (you have 0.27.0 installed), `useAgent` takes a `transport` option. It runs the Agent protocol over one of three transports:

- **`cf-websocket`**: the default.
- **A hibernating WebSocket**: still a WebSocket, but it lets the Durable Object hibernate between messages.
- **`capnweb`**: experimental. It uses Cap'n Web RPC.

So capnweb is the only one that isn't a WebSocket, and it's experimental.

This comes from the project's `.ludion/lessons.md`. That file says the entry hasn't been checked against tests, so look at the agents 0.27.0 types or docs for the exact option values before you rely on them.

No. This project has `agents` 0.27.0 installed, and per the project's Ludion lessons, `subAgent()` has been deprecated since 0.23.0. Use `this.dynamicAgents.get()` in new code. Existing `subAgent()` calls still run without errors, so you can migrate gradually. The related `hasSubAgent()`, `listSubAgents()`, `abortSubAgent()` and `deleteSubAgent()` methods also still work but are deprecated too; they just pass through to `this.dynamicAgents`. That lesson comes from your own ledger and was drafted by an agent without running tests, so check the 0.23.0 changelog or the installed type definitions before you rely on the exact `dynamicAgents` API.

No. In the installed `agents` 0.27.0, `Agent` no longer extends PartyServer's `Server`. It extends Cloudflare's `DurableObject` directly. The compiled package shows `var Agent = class Agent extends DurableObject` at `node_modules/agents/dist/src-DgCbZtIR.js:1531`.

This matches the project's lessons file, which dates the change to agents 0.22.0 and says the PartyServer runtime it needs is now bundled in under `agents/lifecycle`. That lesson hasn't been verified, though, and I only checked the class declaration, not the `agents/lifecycle` part. Existing code that used `Agent` keeps running without errors. If you have code that checks `instanceof Server`, test it, because I'd expect that check to stop matching.

It throttles by default. In the installed `agents` 0.27.0, `useAgentChat` groups streamed updates and re-renders at most every 50ms. You can see it in `node_modules/agents/dist/chat/react.js:15-16`: `throttle === false` turns throttling off, and otherwise it uses `throttle ?? experimental_throttle ?? 50`.

- **To render every chunk as it arrives:** pass `throttle: false` (an explicit `0` also turns it off).
- **To change the interval:** pass a number of milliseconds, such as `throttle: 100`. `experimental_throttle` is still accepted as a deprecated alias.

The project's lessons file says this default arrived in 0.22.0. I only checked the installed 0.27.0 code, not when the change happened.

A scheduled callback gets two arguments: the **payload** you passed to `this.schedule(when, "methodName", payload)` (or `scheduleEvery`), and the **`Schedule` object** for that run. The payload comes back after a JSON round-trip, so only JSON-serializable data survives. The `Schedule` object includes `id`, `callback`, `payload`, `type` (`"scheduled"`, `"delayed"`, `"cron"` or `"interval"`), the run `time`, and `delayInSeconds`, `cron` or `intervalSeconds` depending on the type. So the method signature is `async myTask(data: MyPayload, schedule: Schedule) { ... }`.

I checked this in the installed agents 0.27.0: the scheduler calls `handler(timing.payload, schedule)` (`node_modules/agents/dist/scheduler-DZ3xQfeK.js:229`).

Yes. In the installed `agents` 0.27.0 you can add scheduling to a plain `DurableObject` without extending `Agent`. Create a `Scheduler` from `agents/schedules` and register it with `Lifecycle.install(this).use(this.scheduler)` from `agents/lifecycle`. Lifecycle then owns the Durable Object's alarm and wakes your object for its scheduled tasks. You register named callbacks in the `Scheduler` constructor, create schedules with `set()` and `every()`, and manage them with `get()`, `list()` and `cancel()`. The bundled docs (`node_modules/agents/docs/scheduling.md`) say `Scheduler` and `agents/lifecycle` are **experimental** and may change between releases. Only `Agent`'s own `this.schedule()` methods are called stable, so pin your version if you rely on this.

In the installed `agents` 0.27.0 you can't pass storage to the constructor. Its signature is `new MCPClientManager(name, version, options?)`, and `MCPClientManagerOptions` only accepts `env` (used to restore `rpc://` connections) and `createAuthProvider` (a factory for OAuth). See `node_modules/agents/dist/agent-routing-Bhdbvf7s.d.ts:2743` and `:2799`.

`MCPClientManager` is a `LifecycleCapability`, so it uses the storage of whichever Lifecycle host installs it. Inside an `Agent`, that's the agent's own Durable Object storage, available as `this.mcp`. To have it use your own `DurableObjectStorage`, install it on a Lifecycle in your own Durable Object, and it will use that object's `ctx.storage`. The type comments mark installing it directly on a Lifecycle (outside `agent.mcp`) as experimental. The older pattern of passing `{ storage }` to the constructor no longer exists in this version.

Yes. In the installed agents 0.27.0, `createMcpHandler` (exported from `agents/mcp`) serves an `McpServer` from `@modelcontextprotocol/server` v2. The catch is that you have to pass a factory function, not a server instance.

The parameter type is v2's own `McpServerFactory`, which is `(ctx: McpRequestContext) => McpServer | Server | Promise<McpServer | Server>` (`node_modules/agents/dist/handler-stateless-DxYpJ_XF.d.ts:87`). The handler calls that factory for every request, so concurrent requests each get their own server. A single `McpServer` instance created up front won't type-check. Write `createMcpHandler(() => { const server = new McpServer(...); /* register tools */ return server; })` instead.

I checked this against the type definitions only; I didn't run anything.

In the installed `agents` package (0.27.0), the MCP client sends a `server/discover` request first. It uses the MCP v2 client and works out the protocol version for each connection, then picks one of two paths:

- **Stateless servers** answer `server/discover`, and the client carries on from there.
- **Older servers** (Legacy Streamable HTTP, SSE and RPC) don't answer it, so the client falls back to the classic `initialize` handshake on the same connection.

Older `agents` versions (before 0.20.0) opened with `initialize`. The package's own docs confirm this, in `node_modules/agents/docs/mcp-client.md:191`.

Yes. The installed `agents` 0.27.0 lists `ai` as an optional peer dependency with the range `"^6.0.0 || ^7.0.0"` (`node_modules/agents/package.json:84`). Its own dev setup also builds and tests against `ai` `^7.0.0` (line 60), alongside `@ai-sdk/react` `^4` and `@ai-sdk/provider` `^4`. If you use v7, install the matching companion packages too: `@ai-sdk/react` 4.x (the peer range accepts `^3 || ^4`) and `@ai-sdk/provider` 4.x (the peer range accepts only `^4`). This answer comes from the package's declared ranges. I didn't run anything to test it.

If you leave off the `await`, the `expect(...)` call just hands back a promise, so your test function can finish before the assertion has run. In plain Jest that means a failing assertion may go unnoticed or show up as an unhandled rejection after the test has already passed.

Vitest catches this case. It notices `.resolves`/`.rejects` assertions that were never awaited, prints a warning like "Promise returned by `expect(actual).resolves.toBe(expected)` was not awaited", and awaits them itself when the test ends, so a failure still fails the test. That warning also said a future major version would make a missing `await` an error. I haven't checked whether your installed Vitest 5.0.3 does that yet.

Either way, write `await expect(promise).resolves.toBe(1)` (or `return` it). The `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` lint rule or `vitest/valid-expect` will flag the ones you miss.

No. With the vitest 5.0.3 installed here, Vitest only looks for a config file in the root directory, which is the current working directory unless you pass `--root`. It doesn't walk up into parent folders. The installed code shows this: `findConfigFile` in `node_modules/vitest/dist/chunks/index.DpLw24bj.js:14267` only checks `root/<config name>`, and if nothing is there it returns `false` so Vite won't search either.

Older Vitest versions did search parent directories, so a setup that relied on that can quietly run with no config, and nothing will error. From a subfolder, pass the config explicitly with `vitest --config ../vitest.config.ts`, or set `--root` to the folder that contains it.

Usually no. `vitest` already depends on `@vitest/runner`, and the parts meant for users are re-exported through Vitest itself:

- **Test APIs** like `test`, `describe`, `beforeEach` and `onTestFinished` come from `vitest`.
- **Lower-level runner helpers** like `getCurrentSuite`, `createTaskCollector`, `setFn` and `getFn` come from `vitest/suite`.

Adding `@vitest/runner` yourself can install a second copy whose version doesn't match your `vitest` (5.0.3). If that happens, the runner state isn't shared between the two copies, so hooks and suite context can fail in odd, silent ways. Only add it if you're writing a custom runner or tooling outside Vitest. If you do, pin it to exactly the same version as `vitest`.

This is based on Vitest's general guidance; I didn't check your installed package for this answer.

Yes. With a string argument, `toHaveTextContent` passes if the element's text contains that string, so `expect(el).toHaveTextContent('Hello')` passes for "Hello world". It collapses runs of whitespace before comparing; pass `{ normalizeWhitespace: false }` to turn that off. For an exact match, use an anchored regex such as `toHaveTextContent(/^Hello world$/)`, or compare `el.textContent` with `toBe`.

The matcher isn't built into Vitest's core `expect`. It comes from `@testing-library/jest-dom` (imported via `@testing-library/jest-dom/vitest`), and Vitest browser mode's `expect.element` provides a version that matches substrings the same way. I answered from memory and didn't check it against the docs or your installed vitest 5.0.3.

Yes. In Vitest browser mode, `page.getByText()` and the other text-based locators (`getByRole` with `name`, `getByLabelText`, `getByPlaceholder`, `getByAltText`, `getByTitle`) take an `exact` option that defaults to `false`. With the default, a string matches any element whose text contains it, ignoring case and normalizing whitespace, the same way Playwright does. Pass `{ exact: true }` to require a case-sensitive, whole-string match, or pass a RegExp for full control.

I answered from memory and didn't check it against the vitest 5.0.3 installed here. The project's vitest 5 notes don't mention any change to this behavior.

Use `-t` (or `--testNamePattern`) with a pattern that matches the test's **full name**: the enclosing `describe` names and the test name, joined by spaces, as shown in the reporter output. For example, `it('adds numbers')` inside `describe('math')` is matched as `math adds numbers`, so you'd run `npx vitest -t "math adds numbers"`. Pass a file path too to avoid loading other files, e.g. `npx vitest src/math.test.ts -t "math adds numbers"`. The pattern is a regex, so `-t "^math adds numbers$"` makes it exact and won't also pick up something like `adds numbers twice`.

This project's lessons file says Vitest 5 matches against the full name, but that claim hasn't been tested. If the pattern matches nothing, try just the test name, or check the name your reporter prints.

In the vitest 5.0.3 installed here, `--reporter=blob` writes to **`.vitest/blob/blob.json`** under the project root, unless you set `outputFile`. If you shard the run, the file name gets the shard added, for example `.vitest/blob/blob-1-3.json`. If you set a merge-reports label, that goes in the name too.

This is a change from older versions, which wrote to `.vitest-reports/blob.json`. `--merge-reports` now reads from the same `.vitest/blob` folder by default. If your CI scripts upload or collect `.vitest-reports/`, update those paths.

I confirmed this in the installed package's code (`node_modules/vitest/dist/chunks/index.DpLw24bj.js:15805` and `:15940`), not just in the project's lessons file.

Yes, in the vitest 5.0.3 you have installed. Inline projects in `test.projects` now inherit every option from the root config by default, because `extends` defaults to `true`. I checked this against the installed type definitions (`node_modules/vitest/dist/chunks/plugin.d.BsjqSb4-.d.ts:4499-4507`), which document `extends?: string | boolean` with `@default true`.

This is a silent change from Vitest 3/4. There, an inline project inherited nothing unless you set `extends: true`, so older configs may now pick up root options you didn't expect. To keep a project fully separate, set `extends: false`. You can also set `extends` to a path, such as `'../vite.config.ts'`, to merge the project with that config instead.

Not in a useful way. Vitest hoists `vi.mock` to the top of the file, ahead of all imports, no matter where you write it. Wrapping it in a function or an `if` block doesn't make it conditional, because it runs before your condition is ever evaluated. Recent Vitest versions also print a warning that a nested `vi.mock` will become an error in a future release, so it may already be an error in the vitest 5.0.3 this project uses. I haven't checked that.

If you need conditional or runtime mocking, use `vi.doMock`, which isn't hoisted. It only affects modules you import after it runs, so load the module with `await import(...)`. You can call `vi.resetModules()` first if the module was already loaded.

The vitest 5.0.3 installed here has `vi.when` (I checked its type definitions in `node_modules`). You give it a spy and set a result for each set of arguments:

```ts
const spy = vi.fn()
vi.when(spy).calledWith('darkMode').thenReturn(true)
vi.when(spy).calledWith(expect.any(Number)).thenReturn(0)
vi.when(spy).calledWith('user').thenResolve({ id: 1 })  // async
```

By default, a call with arguments you didn't set up falls through to the spy's original implementation. Pass `{ onUnmatched: 'throw' }` as the second argument to make it throw instead. The classic way works in every Vitest version: branch on the arguments inside `mockImplementation`, e.g. `spy.mockImplementation((key) => key === 'darkMode' ? true : 0)`.

In the vitest version installed here, each call to your function is raced against the poll timeout, which defaults to 1000 ms. If your function's promise hasn't settled when the timeout fires, Vitest stops waiting for it. It also aborts the `AbortSignal` it passes to your function as `fn({ signal })`. You can use that signal to cancel the pending work, such as a fetch.

The assertion then fails and the test does not hang. The error is "expect.poll() function didn't resolve in time.", with a cause of "Matcher did not succeed in time.". If an earlier attempt had already failed, Vitest throws that earlier error instead. Either way, the stack trace points at your `expect.poll(...)` line in the test.

I got this from the installed source (`node_modules/vitest/dist/chunks/index.C4tKZ0yW.js`, around lines 7581–7627), not from running a test. Older Vitest versions did not race the callback this way, so a callback that never resolved could hang until the test's own timeout.

Use the `--repeats` flag, for example `npx vitest run --repeats 10`. It reruns every test the number of times you give it, whether the test passes or fails, so a flaky test will show up as an intermittent failure. I confirmed the flag in this project's installed Vitest CLI, where it's described as "Repeat every test a specific number of times regardless of the result (default: `0`)". Since the default is 0, the number probably counts extra runs after the first, so `--repeats 10` would run each test 11 times. Don't confuse it with `--retry`: that only reruns tests that failed, which hides flakiness instead of exposing it. To focus on one suspect test, add `-t "<pattern>"`. In Vitest 5 the pattern is matched against the full name, meaning the suite names plus the test name.

Yes, `-p` is short for `--project` in the Vitest 5.0.3 installed here. I checked the CLI option definitions in `node_modules/vitest/dist/chunks/cac.DfDGTQ9W.js:1131`, which set `shorthand: "p"` on `project`. Like `--project`, you can repeat it to select several projects (for example, `vitest -p api -p web`). It also takes wildcards (`-p "packages*"`) and `!` to exclude projects. Vitest 4 and earlier don't have this shorthand, so use `--project` there.

No. In the vitest version installed here (5.0.3), `vitest list` reads your test files statically by default and does not run them. I checked this in the installed CLI source: `node_modules/vitest/dist/chunks/cac.DfDGTQ9W.js:1340` defines `staticParse` with `default: true` and the description "Parse files statically instead of running them to collect tests." If you need the older behaviour, pass `--no-static-parse` and it will run the files to collect tests. You might want that if tests are generated at runtime, for example in loops or with dynamic names.
